name: Time4Learning
line: Time4Learning teaches math in a fixed order at a grade the parent picks. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous.
description: AMP vs Time4Learning: math lessons in a fixed sequence at a grade the parent picks, and math where assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Time4Learning is an online homeschool curriculum for every core subject. In math, a learner works through lessons in a fixed sequence, at a grade level the parent chooses [1][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test and no test day. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. It keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. In Time4Learning the parent chooses a grade level for each subject and can change it at any time. Its FAQ suggests starting where a learner begins to have difficulty on a grade's quizzes and tests [1]. Inside a course, lessons follow a fixed scope and sequence that the parent schedules with the Activity Planner [2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Time4Learning the unit is the lesson: video instruction, interactive quizzes and printable worksheets [2]. In grades 6 to 12, filmed instructors teach in short segments [3]. Cathy Duffy's review describes a high school lesson as a presentation by a real person, then practice questions and usually a quiz [5]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [9].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Time4Learning's FAQ does not mention mastery or a passing score [1]. In its grades 6 to 12 Cinema Series, students can retake assessments and the lowest score can be dropped [3].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In Time4Learning, Cathy Duffy's review says, a learner can review earlier topics or retake lessons [5]. We found no scheduled review of earlier skills in its FAQ, its third-grade page or its Cinema Series page [1][2][3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [8].

reasons.title: What the adult does
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. Time4Learning offers no live teachers, and the parent acts as the teacher [1]. The parent picks the grade level in each subject, plans the days with the Activity Planner, reviews reports and grades writing with the scoring guides provided [1][5].

rows.range: PreK through grade 12, every core subject. Math runs through Pre-Calculus and Advanced Math & Trigonometry [3][5].
rows.start: The parent picks a grade level for each subject and can change it at any time. We found no placement test [1].
rows.teaching: Lessons with video instruction, interactive quizzes and printable worksheets [2]. Animated in the early grades; filmed instructors in grades 6 to 12 [5][3].
rows.next: A fixed scope and sequence in each course, scheduled by the parent with the Activity Planner [2].
rows.mastery: No mastery rule found in its FAQ [1]. In grades 6 to 12, assessments can be retaken and the lowest score dropped [3].
rows.review: No scheduled review of earlier skills found in the pages we read [1][2][3].
rows.print: Printable worksheets in each lesson, with answer keys for the parent online and in print [2][1].
rows.adult: The parent teaches: picks the grade level, plans the days with the Activity Planner, reviews reports and grades writing [1][5].
rows.reports: Automatic grading, scores, time per activity and weekly reports [2][5].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its homepage, About page or FAQ, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [10][4][1][6][7].

theirs: Time4Learning is an online homeschool curriculum for PreK through grade 12 that covers every core subject, math among them [3][5]. It is a brand of Cambium Learning Group [4]. It describes itself as a curriculum provider, not an accredited school, and it offers no live teachers [1].

A learner logs in and works through lessons subject by subject, at their own pace, at a grade level the parent chooses for each subject [1][2]. Each lesson has video instruction, interactive quizzes and printable worksheets [2]. Elementary lessons mix animation, pictures, text and activities [5]. In grades 6 to 12, the Cinema Series teaches with filmed instructors in short segments and shows feedback and scores right away [3]. The parent plans the days with the Activity Planner and reviews the reports [1][2].
credit: Filmed instructors teach grades 6 to 12 in short segments [3].
In grades 6 to 12, feedback and scores show right away [3].
A learner can review earlier topics or retake lessons [5].

theirs: We found no study of how much students learn with Time4Learning. Its homepage, About page and FAQ link to no study, it has no entry in Evidence for ESSA, and the What Works Clearinghouse has no intervention report on it [10][4][1][6][7].
ours: The two findings that bear most on this comparison: practice that mixes and spaces topics scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks, in a randomized trial of 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [8], and worked examples improve math performance across 55 studies [9]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want one curriculum for every subject, with math taught in lessons at a grade you choose.
Your middle or high schooler learns well from filmed instructors.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You use Time4Learning for other subjects and want a separate math program beside it.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Time4Learning?
questions.answer: Time4Learning teaches math in lessons that follow a fixed sequence, at a grade level the parent chooses [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Time4Learning work?
questions.answer: We found no study of how much students learn with Time4Learning, on its homepage, About page or FAQ, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [10][4][1][6][7].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs, and a learner can use Time4Learning for other subjects and AMP for math. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
